\[
L(f) = \ln\big(1 + \lvert \mathcal{F} I(f) \rvert\big),
\qquad
P = \Big\{ f : L(f) - \max_{R(f)} L > \tau,\ \lvert f \rvert \ge f_0 \Big\} \oplus D_s,
\quad
B(f) = \operatorname{median}_{R(f)} L,
\qquad
\mathcal{F} I'(f) = \mathcal{F} I(f)\, \frac{e^{B(f)} - 1}{\lvert \mathcal{F} I(f) \rvert}\ \ (f \in P),
\qquad
\tau = 0.5,\ f_0 = 0.1,\ s = 5
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(L\): The log magnitude of the spectrum
- \(R(f)\): The ring of frequency bins around f, from s + 1 to half the ring size away
- \(B\): The background, the median of L on the ring
- \(P\): The peaks, widened by the spread
- \(s\): The peak spread
- \(\tau\): The peak threshold
- \(f_0\): The lowest frequency searched, in cycles per pixel

A halftone screen is a regular grid of dots. In the spectrum, a regular pattern is a set of sharp, isolated peaks at its frequency and its harmonics. The image itself also has strong features in the spectrum, but they are lines and rings: an edge makes a line, a disk makes rings. So the filter compares the log magnitude L at each frequency with the highest value on a ring R(f) around it. The ring runs from s + 1 to half the ring size away. A point on a line or a ring has neighbors on R(f) as high as itself, so only isolated peaks stand above all of R(f). Cores that stand more than tau above, at least f0 cycles per pixel from the center, are widened by a square D_s of s bins. Their magnitude is lowered to B, the median of L on the ring. The phase is kept, so the rest of the image keeps its place. This is a notch filter as in Gonzalez and Woods, with the notches found automatically. The rule for finding peaks is PixelNexus's own. The spectrum is symmetric and every step treats f and -f alike, so the result is real.
